articles.title: Maladaptive daydreaming is linked to social media addiction and hypersexuality
articles.summary: People who spend excessive time lost in vivid, immersive fantasies often report higher rates of social media addiction and hypersexuality. New research suggests that underlying narcissistic traits and fragile self-esteem may connect these compulsive behaviors.

articles.title: New study links the spread of the internet to a global decline in religious identity
articles.summary: As internet access spreads across the globe, formal religious affiliation tends to fall. A new study of 81 countries links three decades of digital expansion to a steady decline in traditional religious identity.

articles.title: These blood thinners may have an unexpected benefit for Alzheimer’s patients
articles.summary: Newer blood thinners may do more than prevent strokes in people with Alzheimer’s disease and atrial fibrillation. Researchers found that patients taking NOACs experienced a slower decline in cognitive function than those using warfarin or no blood thinners. The effect was modest each year but could add up over time.

articles.title: Textbooks may have misdrawn this basic brain structure for 100 years
articles.summary: Scientists discovered that brain-cell axons may not be smooth tubes as textbooks have shown for more than a century, but instead naturally resemble strings of tiny pearls. Those pearl-like structures can change with neural activity and may help control how quickly electrical signals travel through the brain.

articles.title: Esketamine-induced dissociation is tied to better outcomes in treatment-resistant depression
articles.summary: Patients with treatment-resistant depression who experienced feelings of unreality during subcutaneous esketamine therapy were more likely to see their depression symptoms improve, suggesting dissociation may be tied to the drug's effectiveness rather than just a side effect.

articles.title: Scientists find that “perfect” systems may be surprisingly fragile
articles.summary: Complex systems may work better when their parts are not perfectly alike. Northwestern physicists found that carefully balanced variation, or “disorder,” can make networks such as power grids, ecosystems, neurons, and materials more stable. Even random differences sometimes improved stability compared with completely uniform systems. The discovery could help researchers design more resilient technologies and explain why natural systems are so rarely perfectly uniform.

articles.title: Memories of childhood scents associated with joy are encoded by neurons generated shortly after birth
articles.summary: A new study reveals that powerful, happy childhood scent memories are encoded by neurons generated just after birth. As we age, the brain reorganizes how it stores these smells, shifting from reward centers to deeper emotional networks.

articles.summary: Can implicit bias tests predict how people actually behave? A new adversarial collaboration finds that while indirect tests capture a tiny fraction of hidden bias, traditional self-report surveys are vastly superior at predicting race-related decisions.

articles.title: Learning about the opposing party’s vaccination rate influences health choices
articles.summary: Public health campaigns often broadcast low vaccination rates to encourage people to get their shots. A recent experiment suggests this strategy might backfire, showing that people adjust their healthcare decisions based on the behavior of opposing political groups.

articles.title: Puberty, pregnancy, and menopause are accompanied by distinct patterns of brain plasticity
articles.summary: A new brain imaging study indicates that puberty and pregnancy are associated with widespread gray matter reductions in the female brain. In contrast, the menopausal transition coincides with a surprising pause in typical age-related brain changes.

articles.summary: An experimental brain cancer treatment using a modified measles virus becomes more effective in mice when combined with a common antidepressant, which helps release trapped immune cells from the bone marrow to fight the tumor.

articles.summary: A large analysis of children's brain scans reveals that socioeconomic status is the primary factor shaping brain organization. The findings suggest that brain patterns previously linked to intelligence actually reflect environmental factors like stress and sleep deprivation.

articles.title: Why relying on university students skews global psychological research
articles.summary: A new study of 95 countries reveals that higher education—not wealth—makes individuals globally more culturally similar to Western nations. This raises concerns about the accuracy of psychological research that relies heavily on university students.
